Westminster Directory for Public Worship
WEST-min-ster di-REK-tuh-ree
historical document
From the Westminster Assembly and directory (a guide of directions, rather than a fixed prescribed form); the Assembly’s guide for worship.

Biblical Definition

The Westminster Directory for the Public Worship of God is the guide for worship produced by the Westminster Assembly in 1645, intended to replace the Book of Common Prayer in the churches of England, Scotland, and Ireland. Unlike a prescribed liturgy that fixes every word to be read, the Directory offered directions—a framework of guidance for the ordering and conduct of worship, leaving the minister to lead in his own words within scriptural bounds. It set forth directions for the assembling of the congregation, public prayer, the reading and preaching of the Word (with a notable treatment of the right method of preaching), the administration of baptism and the Lord’s Supper, the sanctification of the Lord’s Day, the solemnization of marriage, the visitation of the sick, burial of the dead, and the singing of psalms. It embodied the Puritan and Reformed conviction that worship is to be governed by the Word and conducted with reverence, simplicity, and edification, free from the imposed forms and ceremonies the Puritans judged unwarranted. The dictionary honors the Westminster Directory as a faithful expression of Reformed worship in the British tradition, a companion to the Westminster Confession and Catechisms, embodying the regulative principle in practice. It stands as a model of worship directed rather than dictated—ordered by Scripture, reverent in conduct, centered on the Word and prayer and psalmody—and remains a valued guide in the Presbyterian and broader Reformed churches that trace their heritage to the Assembly.

The Westminster Assembly’s 1645 guide for worship, offering directions rather than a fixed liturgy, embodying the regulative principle in the British Reformed tradition.

Modern Corruption

Worship is either bound again by imposed forms or left to careless disorder, against the Directory’s ordered freedom under the Word.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is worship directed by Scripture rather than dictated by imposed forms or left to careless disorder. The Directory replaced the fixed prescriptions of the Prayer Book with a framework of scriptural guidance, trusting the minister to lead in his own words within godly bounds. It embodies the regulative principle: worship ordered by the Word, reverent in conduct, centered on prayer, preaching, and psalmody, free of unwarranted ceremony.

Where a corruption presses, it presses from two directions, as it did in the seventeenth century and does still. On one side stands the imposition of fixed liturgical forms upon the conscience, the very burden the Puritans labored to remove; on the other stands a careless disorder that, despising all guidance, conducts worship without reverence, preparation, or edification. The dictionary commends the Directory’s wise middle path: not a script that binds, nor a vacuum that breeds chaos, but ordered freedom under the Word—reverent, simple, intelligible worship, directed by Scripture and conducted to the glory of God and the building up of His people.
